title: Numerical Methods and Scientific Computing
description: A concrete-first bridge from linear systems and finite precision to differential equations and optimization.

modules.title: Mathematician pathway
modules.description: Derive algorithms, justify transformations, and analyze error.

modules.title: Mathematics programmer pathway
modules.description: Implement exact and numerical methods with reproducible tests.

modules.title: Computational hacker pathway
modules.description: Experiment with solver behavior, boundary cases, and measured performance.

objectives.title: Linear systems and Gaussian elimination
objectives.description: A linear system describes several constraints on unknown quantities. Matrix notation makes the structure visible, and Gaussian elimination applies row operations that preserve the solution set. Exact arithmetic clarifies the mathematics; floating-point arithmetic adds numerical considerations.

objectives.title: Floating-point error and numerical stability
objectives.description: Computers represent most real numbers with finite precision. Rounding error can accumulate or cancel significant digits. Conditioning describes sensitivity of the mathematical problem; stability describes how an algorithm behaves in the presence of finite-precision error.

objectives.title: Differential equations and numerical integration
objectives.description: A differential equation links a system's state to its rate of change. An initial value problem specifies a starting state. Numerical methods such as Euler and Runge-Kutta approximate a trajectory; step size, stability, and error controls determine whether the approximation is useful.

objectives.title: Optimization and gradient methods
objectives.description: Optimization chooses decision variables to improve an objective while respecting constraints. Gradients indicate local directions of increase; gradient descent moves in the opposite direction. Convergence depends on the objective's geometry, step size, initialization, and constraints.

lessons.title: Linear systems and Gaussian elimination
lessons.body: A linear system describes several constraints on unknown quantities. Matrix notation makes the structure visible, and Gaussian elimination applies row operations that preserve the solution set. Exact arithmetic clarifies the mathematics; floating-point arithmetic adds numerical considerations.
lessons.historical_context: Gaussian elimination is named for Carl Friedrich Gauss, though systematic elimination methods have older roots. Matrix notation later made linear systems a central language for geometry, physics, and computation.

stages.prompt: Three products have prices that satisfy two budget equations. Ask whether the equations determine one combination, many combinations, or none.
Solve a small two-equation system by substitution, then compare with elimination. Notice which operations preserve the solutions.
Represent the system as intersecting lines and as an augmented matrix. Label pivots and free variables.
Explain pivot, row operation, rank, inconsistent system, and free variable.
Write an augmented matrix and justify each elementary row operation as an equivalence-preserving transformation.
Implement exact rational Gaussian elimination and test unique, infinite, and no-solution cases.

exercise.objective: Solve and classify a linear system using row reduction.
exercise.prompt: Solve 2x+y=5 and x-y=1 using an augmented matrix. Show each row operation, state the solution, and explain how the pivot structure would change if the second equation were 2x+y=7.
hints: Write the augmented matrix with one row per equation.
Use a row operation to eliminate x or y from one row.
Compare the final contradiction or pivot structure in the modified system.

rubric.description: Performs valid row operations and obtains the solution.
Explains pivot structure and classification.
Distinguishes exact rational solving from numerical rounding.
Classifies the modified system.

exercise.transfer_prompt: Give a 3-variable system with infinitely many solutions and identify its free variable.

lessons.title: Floating-point error and numerical stability
lessons.body: Computers represent most real numbers with finite precision. Rounding error can accumulate or cancel significant digits. Conditioning describes sensitivity of the mathematical problem; stability describes how an algorithm behaves in the presence of finite-precision error.
lessons.historical_context: Numerical analysis grew alongside scientific computing. Wilkinson's work on numerical stability helped establish why a mathematically equivalent formula may behave very differently on a computer.

stages.prompt: Try to store one third as a finite decimal. Multiplying the stored approximation by three may not return exactly one.
Compare two algebraically equivalent expressions for a small difference of squares when x is large and y is close to x.
Draw a number line with representable floating-point values becoming farther apart as magnitude grows.
Explain rounding error, cancellation, conditioning, stability, precision, and tolerance.
Distinguish forward error from backward error and relate problem conditioning to algorithm stability.
Run a reproducible cancellation experiment against exact rational arithmetic. Record precision, inputs, and error.

exercise.objective: Identify cancellation and distinguish conditioning from algorithmic stability.
exercise.prompt: Compare (sqrt(x+1)-sqrt(x)) with 1/(sqrt(x+1)+sqrt(x)) for x=10^16 using floating-point arithmetic. Explain why the second form is more stable, and describe how you would compare both against a higher-precision reference.
hints: Rationalize the first expression by multiplying numerator and denominator by the conjugate.
The exact expressions are equal, but the subtraction may lose significant digits.
State the reference precision and error metric before comparing.

rubric.description: Explains cancellation and why algebraic equivalence does not imply equal numerical behavior.
Derives the rationalized expression correctly.
Distinguishes conditioning from algorithm stability and names an error metric.
Suggests a reproducible precision-controlled comparison.

exercise.transfer_prompt: Find another pair of equivalent formulas where one is numerically more stable and explain why.

lessons.title: Differential equations and numerical integration
lessons.body: A differential equation links a system's state to its rate of change. An initial value problem specifies a starting state. Numerical methods such as Euler and Runge-Kutta approximate a trajectory; step size, stability, and error controls determine whether the approximation is useful.
lessons.historical_context: Euler developed early numerical methods for differential equations. Runge and Kutta later developed higher-order methods that are widely used in scientific simulation.

stages.prompt: Model a growing bacterial population whose growth rate is proportional to its current size. The state changes continuously, but a computer advances in finite steps.
Use a small step to estimate y'=y with y(0)=1. Compare the first Euler step with the exact value e^h.
Plot Euler and RK4 approximations against y=e^t. Show how reducing step size changes the trajectory.
Explain initial condition, derivative function, step size, local truncation error, global error, and stability.
Write the Euler update and the four RK4 slope evaluations. State the assumptions needed for the initial value problem.
Implement Euler and RK4 with a fixed step grid. Record solver, step size, seed if used, runtime, and error against the exact solution.

exercise.objective: Compare numerical ODE methods against a known solution.
exercise.prompt: For y'=y with y(0)=1 on [0,1], compute one Euler step and one RK4 step with h=1. Compare both with e, then explain why this single large step is illustrative rather than a convergence study.
hints: RK4 combines four slope estimates at the beginning, midpoint, and end of the interval.
Compare absolute errors and state that convergence requires a sequence of step sizes.

rubric.description: States the initial value problem and exact solution.
Computes Euler and RK4 updates correctly.
Explains the role of step size and method order.
Designs a step-refinement experiment.

exercise.transfer_prompt: Repeat with h=1/2 and h=1/4. Predict how the global errors should change for Euler and RK4.

lessons.title: Optimization and gradient methods
lessons.body: Optimization chooses decision variables to improve an objective while respecting constraints. Gradients indicate local directions of increase; gradient descent moves in the opposite direction. Convergence depends on the objective's geometry, step size, initialization, and constraints.
lessons.historical_context: Lagrange developed methods for constrained optimization. Cauchy introduced an early gradient method; modern optimization connects calculus, linear algebra, statistics, and machine learning.

stages.prompt: Choose a point on a hilly landscape and try to walk downhill. The local slope suggests a direction, but the route depends on step length.
For f(x)=(x-3)^2, start at x=0 and take repeated steps opposite the derivative. Compare small and large step sizes.
Plot the objective and mark successive iterates. Show overshooting when the step size is too large.
Explain objective, feasible set, gradient, stationary point, local optimum, and global optimum.
Write x_(k+1)=x_k-η∇f(x_k). State conditions under which a convex quadratic has a unique global minimizer.
Implement gradient descent with recorded initialization, step size, stopping tolerance, and iteration limit. Compare against the analytic solution.

exercise.objective: Apply gradient descent and explain the effect of step size.
exercise.prompt: For f(x)=(x-3)^2, derive the gradient update and perform three iterations from x0=0 with η=0.1. Repeat conceptually with η=1.1 and explain the difference in behavior.
hints: Substitute the derivative into the update rule and compute each iterate.
For this quadratic, η=1 reaches the minimizer in one step; larger values may overshoot or oscillate.

rubric.description: Defines the objective and minimizer correctly.
Computes the three updates accurately.
Explains step-size effects on convergence.
Identifies what changes for a non-convex objective.

exercise.transfer_prompt: Change the objective to f(x)=x^4-2x^2. Explain why a local gradient method may depend on its starting point.
